redis the smallest type stores nothing permanently
postgres 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM; from about 60 active people 4 vCPU, 8 GB, ideally with dedicated vCPUs or one of the options below
– Network: under Networks, create a private network (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16) and attach every server and the load balancer. Flowplan, Redis and PostgreSQL listen on their private address only.
– Placement group: put app-1 and app-2 into a placement group of type spread, so they do not run on the same physical host.

– Firewall: one Cloud Firewall for every server: inbound only TCP 22 from your address. The app servers need no public ports – the load balancer reaches them through the private network. The Cloud Firewall only applies to the public interface, so protect Redis and PostgreSQL with a password as well and bind them to the private address (Docker bypasses ufw).

en.heading: Object Storage
paragraphs: Under Object Storage, create a private bucket in the same location and create a key under S3 credentials (the secret is shown only once). Endpoint and region follow the location, e.g. S3_ENDPOINT=https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com and S3_REGION=fsn1 – use the endpoint the console shows for your bucket. With FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, files and backups are stored there encrypted.

en.heading: PostgreSQL
paragraphs: Option The database server fails Effort
One PostgreSQL server with backups (postgres.yaml in the example) Flowplan is down until the server runs again or is rebuilt from the backup low: one server, backups as below
Patroni on three small servers with etcd, HAProxy locally on every app server another server takes over within seconds high: run and monitor Patroni, etcd and HAProxy

Managed service of a provider with a data centre nearby the provider switches over low, but the database sits outside the private network: only with TLS (sslmode=require) and access only from your servers' addresses

If Hetzner offers no managed PostgreSQL in your location, pick a provider nearby – every query travels that distance. How Flowplan handles a failover and which address belongs in DATABASE_URL is under Failover and replicas. With Patroni, DATABASE_URL points to 127.0.0.1:5000, where HAProxy offers only the primary.

en.heading: Redis
paragraphs: A small server with redis.yaml from the example: a password, no persistence, on the private address only. A managed Redis with a fixed address works too (rediss:// with TLS); Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster do not. With FLOWPLAN_READY_REQUIRE=database,objectStorage (as in .env.example), Flowplan stays ready while Redis is briefly away.

en.heading: Load balancer
paragraphs: Under Load Balancers, create a load balancer in the same location (the smallest type is enough) and attach it to the private network:
Setting Value
Targets app-1 and app-2, through the private network
Service HTTPS, port 443 → destination port 3000; a certificate managed by Hetzner (Let's Encrypt; the DNS zone must be at Hetzner for that) or one you upload
HTTP → HTTPS switch the redirect on
Health check HTTP, port 3000, path /api/health/ready, every 5–10 seconds, timeout 5 seconds, status 200
Sticky sessions off – not needed
Proxy protocol off
Algorithm round robin or least connections

The load balancer sets X-Forwarded-For, which is why .env has FLOWPLAN_TRUSTED_PROXIES=1. Live connections are server-sent events: the load balancer has to pass them through unbuffered, and Flowplan sends a heartbeat regularly so they are not closed for silence. After setting up, check that a second person's changes appear at once and that a large import (up to 100 MB) goes through. Finally point your domain's A and AAAA records at the load balancer's addresses.

en.heading: Setting up the app servers
paragraphs: – Install Docker following the official guide.
– Get the example files: git clone https://github.com/yannicschuller/flowplan.git and copy what is in deploy/compose/hetzner to /opt/flowplan.
– Create the keys once – openssl rand -base64 32 for FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY, npx web-push generate-vapid-keys for the push keys – and keep a copy apart from the backups.
– cp .env.example .env and fill it in: domain, database, Redis, bucket, keys, setup token. .env is the same on both app servers except for PRIVATE_IP and FLOWPLAN_INSTANCE_ID.
– docker compose up -d on app-1 first, once it is ready on app-2; then create the first account at https:///register?setup=.

en.heading: Backups
paragraphs: – Switch on the scheduled backup under Administration → Storage & backup: the leading instance writes a pg_dump archive into the bucket under /backups/ daily (or hourly), encrypted with FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY (Backups with pg_dump).
– A second copy outside the bucket, e.g. via SFTP to a Hetzner Storage Box – a fault in the bucket then does not hit both.
– The database server additionally with Hetzner's backups (images of the disk); with Patroni, or to restore to any point in time, WAL archiving (e.g. pgBackRest) into a bucket of its own.
– The app servers hold nothing that is not in the bucket or the database – a new server with the same .env replaces an old one.

en.heading: Updates
paragraphs: – Read the release notes and set FLOWPLAN_VERSION in .env on both servers to the new version.
– On app-1: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d. The old instance answers 503, the load balancer takes it out, and the new one brings the schema up to date.
– Wait until the load balancer shows app-1 as healthy again (or curl http://:3000/api/health/ready).
– The same on app-2.
To be on the safe side, remove the server as a target in the load balancer before step 2 and add it back afterwards. The deployment id makes sure browsers do not mix both versions in the meantime.

en.heading: Next
paragraphs: – Cluster mode: every requirement and variable.
– PostgreSQL: failover, replicas and time limits.
– Sizing: how many instances and which hardware.
– Kubernetes: the same with the Helm chart.
Content comes in as Markdown, CSV or an archive and goes out again as Markdown, PDF or a complete archive. The version history brings back earlier states.
More on this topic: Export · Printing and PDF

en.heading: Import
paragraphs: All imports are under Settings → Import & export → Import; at the top you choose the Target space once for all of them.

– Markdown, text or HTML: Markdown, text or HTML files. Headings, lists, tasks, tables, code and formulas become blocks; Mermaid code ( `mermaid , in HTML ` or ) becomes a code block that shows the diagram – the code is one click away (preview). This applies to every import, including AFFiNE, Notion, Obsidian, Confluence (the language of code macros) and pasted Markdown. Image titles and Table:/Listing: lines become captions, in HTML / and `. The AFFiNE import takes over the captions of images and code blocks.

– Notion, AppFlowy or Markdown export: Notion, AppFlowy or Markdown export (ZIP) accepts a ZIP with Markdown and CSV files. Markdown becomes pages, CSV databases, days of a Flowplan journal (…/2026/10/2026-10-27.md below the journal) days of that journal again, Excalidraw and draw.io files whiteboards, folders sub-pages; linked images and files are uploaded, and Notion record pages are matched to their records. A Markdown export from Flowplan (a page or a space as ZIP) comes back with its page tree, titles and databases including their records; comments and earlier versions in the export are left out. Up to 100 MB, by default 10,000 pages (FLOWPLAN_IMPORT_MAX_DOCS) and 5,000 records per table; single files in the ZIP may be as large as the largest upload (at least 10 MB), and ZIPs inside it – such as the “Export-…-Part-1.zip” of large Notion exports – are unpacked too, as long as everything together fits the import's limits. You choose the target space beforehand.
– Jira or Trello: Jira or Trello – see Projects, tickets and sprints.
– {since=0.10.0} Anki: a deck (.apkg) or the collection (.colpkg) becomes flashcard databases – see Import and export flashcards.

– CSV: in a database, choose Import CSV or Markdown and pick a CSV file; the rows become records. A CSV exported from Flowplan comes back as it was: text that looks like a formula (=…, +…, @…) gets a protective apostrophe on export, which the import removes again; tags containing a comma (such as “Night, Weekend”) stay one tag when the column's options include it. The import finds people, related records, files and sprints by their name (people also by e-mail address) and links them again – but only when the name is unique: if two records are called “Meeting”, the cell stays empty rather than linking the wrong one. Columns missing from the file are left out instead of being emptied.

– Reading values: empty number cells stay empty (not 0), so sums and filters such as "is empty" still match after re-importing. Numbers may use a decimal comma and thousands separators ("1,5", "1.234,56"), checkboxes may also read Yes/No, x or ✓, dates also 05.11.2026. A file with a single column (say, a view that shows only the title), short rows and trailing commas work too; only a broken quote makes the file unreadable.
– If a value does not fit a number, date or checkbox property (such as "2026-02-30"), Flowplan refuses the import and names the property – instead of dropping the value or storing it as text.

– New options: values that a select or multi-select property does not have as options yet are added as new options; a different letter case uses the existing option. At most 100 new options per import – a free-text column mapped to a select property is refused rather than creating thousands of options. A notice says which options were added to which property.
– Markdown with frontmatter into a database (such as notes from Obsidian): in the database, choose Import CSV or Markdown and pick one or more .md files or a ZIP – see below.
– Content archive (see below).

en.heading: Frontmatter: records as Markdown files
paragraphs: Notes from Obsidian, Logseq, Jekyll or Hugo carry their properties as YAML frontmatter at the top of the file:
para: Resource
area: House
tags: [heating, maintenance]
# Heating – maintenance

Import into a database: every file becomes a record. The title comes from title:, otherwise from the first # heading or the file name; the rest of the text becomes the record's document, linked images and files from the ZIP are uploaded, and links between the imported files become links to the new records. Keys are matched to properties of the same name (case does not matter):
– select and multi-select take the values and add unknown ones as new options (so tags: lands in Tags);
– relations find the linked record by its title (also as [[Title]]), people by name or e-mail;
– dates are read as ISO dates, true/false as checkboxes, numbers as numbers;

– aliases: (a list or one text, separated by commas) and alias: together fill the property of type Aliases, whatever its name; if there is none, Create missing properties adds one. A database without an aliases property but with a property named "aliases" gets the values there, as before;
– computed properties (formulas, rollups, timestamps) are not overwritten.

When importing records (Markdown, CSV) into a multi-select with the workspace's tags, the values stay names; missing tags are created if you may create tags (members with edit rights) – otherwise such values are left out.

Before the import, a preview shows which properties match and which are missing. Create missing properties adds them with a fitting type: list → multi-select, ISO date → date, true/false → checkbox, number → number, address → URL, a few recurring values → select, otherwise text. Up to 5,000 files and 100 MB per import.

Export: in the ZIP export, every record under records/ starts with title: and its properties: select as text, multi-select and relations (titles of the linked records) as lists, dates as ISO dates. Aliases are written under Obsidian's key aliases: as a list, so they survive a trip to Obsidian and back. Computed values and the record's id are below flowplan: and are skipped on import. When a record exported this way is imported into the same database again, the preview offers update instead of adding: the record with the same id gets the file's properties and text, and the previous state stays as a version. Without this choice it is added as a new record.

Pages: a page's aliases, tags and properties are written by the Markdown export (single page, space export, scheduled export and Git export) as frontmatter at the top of the file – the way Obsidian reads them:
tags:
- Customer
- Offer
Status: Sent
Budget: 12500
Owner: Emil Example
# Offer Müller Ltd
People appear by name, multi-selects as a list, checkboxes as true/false; the automatic properties (created at …) are left out. Pages without aliases, tags and values keep no frontmatter.

When importing Markdown files, Markdown ZIPs and Obsidian vaults under Settings → Import & export, aliases:/alias: becomes the new page's aliases and tags: (or tag:, as a list or “a, b”) its tags; missing tags are created. Further keys become properties: if the workspace already has a property with that name, the page gets its value there. Unknown keys are created as new properties only by workspace owners – the type follows the value (true → checkbox, number → number, 2026-12-01 → date, list → multi-select, URL, email, otherwise text). Keys of publishing tools (cssclass, publish, permalink, layout, slug, draft …) never become properties. When the whole frontmatter is taken over, it disappears from the text; otherwise it stays in the text as before. The Git export reads aliases, tags and values of changed pages back from the repository.

Where to export: in a database's toolbar, Export opens a menu with CSV (current view), Markdown with files (.zip), Markdown (.md) and As Word (DOCX). A single record is exported from the … menu in its header: Export as Markdown (.md) (with frontmatter), Markdown with files (.zip), As Word (DOCX) (properties as a table, then the document) or Print / PDF – with the same print options; Properties there means the record's fields.

CSV (current view) writes the view's visible columns in their order (board, gallery and other card views always with the title) and the values as the table shows them: people (also Created by / Edited by) by name, related records by title, uploaded files by name (links stay links), sprints by name. Numbers, dates and checkboxes are written as stored. If a person's name isn't unique, their e-mail address is written instead. The CSV in the Markdown ZIP still holds all properties.

From Obsidian: links in the text are read as standard Markdown links. Convert wikilinks ([[…]], ![[…]]) first – in Obsidian, Settings → Files and links, turn off “Use [[Wikilinks]]” and choose relative paths.

en.heading: Content archive
paragraphs: Under Settings → Import & export → Export → Workspace as ZIP you download a ZIP of your workspace. To bring it back – also into another Flowplan instance – use Backups → Restore a Flowplan archive: the archive is created as a copy in new private spaces.

Backing up the whole instance (with accounts and permissions) is up to the administration: Administration → Storage & backup. The card Trash & retention leads to the trash and says how long things are kept: deleted pages and spaces until someone deletes them permanently, deleted database records 30 days; how long earlier versions stay is set by the administration.

It contains: accessible pages including the trash, databases with views and records, document content, relations, templates, comments, versions, favourites and form options, plus all files with checksums. Also the settings of databases (done rule, workflow, automations, sprints, story points – never the Git token), time entries and the status history behind burndown charts, the settings and trackers of journals with each day's values and place, handwriting on PDFs and your home page (applied only when the person importing has none of their own yet).

The workspace's tags and properties (unused ones too) and every page's tags and values come along as well. Importing creates missing tags, and missing properties only if you own the target workspace; existing ones with the same name are reused.

The workspace's appearance with its uploaded fonts and its automatic links come along as well (the JSON export holds both, without the font files): on restore only an owner of the target workspace takes them over – link rules in addition to the existing ones (an existing rule with the same pattern stays, at most 50), the appearance only where Flowplan's own look still applies. Whatever fails the settings' checks (an invalid rule, not a font file, over 5 MB, more than 20 fonts, storage quota full) is left out and counted in the message without stopping the import.

The archive only holds what you may see yourself: other people's private records with their comments and files are left out, as are journals behind a PIN you have not unlocked right now. Versions of a database are included only for owners, because they contain every record. Each version holds the whole database; when not all of them fit into the archive of a large database, the newest come along and older ones stay behind – the current records are always included.
– Importing creates new IDs; internal links and relations are rewritten – embedded whiteboards, synced blocks, metrics, drawing blocks and records on whiteboard cards too.
– If the archive comes from someone else, their assignments and mentions become yours; tasks in documents show under My tasks right away.
– Older archives import as before; older servers skip what they do not know.
– Imported spaces and templates are private, shares and forms are not active.
– A failed import is rolled back completely.

– Limits: 2 GB ZIP, 20,000 files, 50,000 pages, 200,000 records per database and 64 MB for pages, records, comments and versions without the files (the file flowplan.json in the archive) – depending on the content, enough for around 100,000 records. The same limit applies to export, import and restore; database versions only go along as long as they fit.
Accounts, sessions and sign-in are not part of it – operations back them up every day with the whole instance.

en.heading: Version history
paragraphs: Page actions → Version history:
– Documents save automatically at most every five minutes, databases before the first change after ten quiet minutes.
– Save current version creates a state at any time; manually saved versions are kept permanently.
– Changes compares a version with the current state or with any other version (Compare with): added and removed text, for databases new, changed and removed records and properties.

– The comparison in detail: it walks the document block by block – headings, paragraphs, list items, table cells, quotes and code stay recognisable as such – and marks the single words inside a changed block: additions green, deletions red and struck through; unchanged blocks are dimmed. A summary states how many words came and went (for example "+120 words · −35 words"), and the arrows jump from change to change, also by keyboard. The same applies to the versions of a record document. Very long documents (more than 60,000 words on both sides together) or versions that differ in too many places are reported as too large to compare; they can still be restored.

– Bring back single paragraphs: compared with the current state, every removed or changed paragraph has a Restore button. The paragraph returns to its old place with its formatting; the rest of the page stays as it is.
– Restore sets the page back to that state. The authors view then starts over; the restored text appears as "earlier".

– Databases come back with properties, options and records – and with the settings that name options: done rule, workflow, automations and the issue sync's status mapping, as they were then. So restoring the version from before an option rename doesn't leave the done rule on the new name. An automation that comes back changed then acts for the person who restored it. Older and imported versions leave the settings as they are.
Automatic versions are thinned out to one per day after seven days and deleted after 180 days (adjustable in the administration).
Workspace owners create addresses with Create address under Settings → General → Inbound e-mail that file incoming e-mail in Flowplan:

– Target page: every e-mail becomes a new subpage. The subject is the title, the text (cleaned HTML or plain text) the content, with sender and date above it. Attachments become files of the new page; embedded images (cid:) appear in place, all other attachments as a list below.

– Target database: every e-mail becomes a record. The subject is the title, the text the record's content, the sender address goes into the first e-mail property (if there is one), the e-mail's date is the creation date, and attachments go into the first files property (otherwise as a list into the content).
– Allowed senders: addresses (ada@example.org) or domains (example.org, exactly that domain). E-mails from other senders are not stored but noted in the audit log.
– Signing key (optional): see below.
The address acts with the permissions of the person who created it. If they lose write access to the target or the target is locked, the address stops accepting mail (the list shows the error).
Security and limits:
– Every address has a random 32-character token. Generate a new token invalidates the current address at once.
– HTML from e-mails is cleaned like guest content: no scripts, forms, styles or frames; remote images (e.g. tracking pixels) are removed, links stay.

– Attachments: at most 20 per e-mail, 10 MB per file, 25 MB together; larger ones are named in the text. The file type is checked against the content, photos lose their location; only images and PDFs open in the browser, everything else is downloaded. Attachments count towards the workspace's storage quota and the daily budget for anonymous uploads (200 MB per address and day, plus FLOWPLAN_ANONYMOUS_UPLOAD_MB for the whole instance).
– At most 60 e-mails per address and hour (rejected ones count too); beyond that Flowplan answers 429 and the provider retries later.
– The same Message-ID is stored only once per address. Without a Message-ID, sender, subject, date and text count.
– The sender address of an e-mail can be forged. The sender list is a pre-filter; above all the token must stay secret. For webhooks the signing key adds protection.

en.heading: Via webhook (Mailgun, Postmark, SendGrid, Cloudflare)
paragraphs: Without further setup Flowplan accepts e-mail as a POST to the webhook address shown in the list:
https://flowplan.example.com/api/inbound-mail/<token>
Flowplan recognises the format from the content:
Provider Setup

Mailgun Receiving → Create Route: an expression such as match_recipient("flowplan@mg.example.com"), action Forward to the webhook address. Enter Mailgun's HTTP webhook signing key as the signing key; Flowplan then checks timestamp, token and signature (at most 15 minutes old).
Postmark Server → Inbound stream → Webhook URL = the webhook address. Postmark sends JSON with FromFull, TextBody, HtmlBody and Attachments.

SendGrid Settings → Inbound Parse → Add Host & URL: domain and webhook address. With POST the raw, full MIME message the whole e-mail arrives (email), otherwise the fields from, subject, text, html, attachment-info and attachment1….
Cloudflare Email Routing An Email Worker rule that passes on the raw e-mail (example below).

Your own scripts JSON or multipart/form-data with from, to, subject, text, html, messageId, date and attachments (JSON: [{ "filename", "contentType", "content" (base64), "contentId" }], multipart: file fields) – or the whole e-mail as raw (text) or rawBase64, or as the body with Content-Type: message/rfc822.
Cloudflare Email Worker:
export default {
async email(message, env) {
const raw = await new Response(message.raw).arrayBuffer();
const body = new Uint8Array(raw);
const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", new TextEncoder().encode(env.FLOWPLAN_KEY), { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]);
const sig = [...new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", key, body))].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");
const res = await fetch(env.FLOWPLAN_URL, {
method: "POST",
headers: { "Content-Type": "message/rfc822", "X-Flowplan-Signature": `sha256=${sig}` },
body,
if (!res.ok) message.setReject(`Flowplan: ${res.status}`);

Signing key: when an address has one, every delivery needs either the header X-Flowplan-Signature: sha256= (HMAC-SHA256 of the unchanged body with the key, as with Flowplan's own webhooks) or Mailgun's signature fields. Otherwise Flowplan answers 401.

Answers: 200 with {"status": "stored" "duplicate" "rejected"} – rejected and duplicate e-mails get 200 too, so the provider does not retry. 401 invalid signature, 404 unknown token, 409 target not writable, 413 too large or daily budget reached, 415 unknown format, 429 hourly limit.

en.heading: Via an IMAP mailbox
paragraphs: Instead of a provider, Flowplan can poll a mailbox of your own (every two minutes, unread e-mail). The administrators set INBOUND_IMAP_HOST, INBOUND_IMAP_USER, INBOUND_IMAP_PASSWORD and INBOUND_MAIL_DOMAIN for it (Configuration). Each address in the list then reads
inbox+<token>@mail.example.com

(plus addressing: the part before + is the mailbox's user name). Flowplan looks for the token in To, Cc, Delivered-To and X-Original-To. Processed, duplicate, rejected and unroutable e-mails are marked as read; when the hourly limit or daily budget is reached they stay unread for the next round.

en.heading: Via the API
paragraphs: With an owner's write token: GET /api/inbound-mail?workspace= lists the addresses; POST /api/command with inbound.save (create or change: pageId, senders, optionally label, secret, id), inbound.rotate and inbound.delete manages them.
Flowplan runs as a single container with SQLite and a data directory. Postgres, Redis or a separate search service are not needed – PostgreSQL and several instances are possible, but optional.

en.heading: Requirements
paragraphs: – A server with Docker and a persistent volume. Text recognition for scanned PDFs briefly needs noticeable CPU when uploading.
– Already running an instance on another server? Then move it after installing instead of starting over.
– A domain with HTTPS through a reverse proxy (Traefik, Caddy, nginx, Coolify, Pangolin …). For just trying it out it works without, see Without HTTPS.
– Optionally an OpenID Connect provider for single sign-on. Without one, people sign in with e-mail and password or a passkey, see Sign-in.
– Optionally an S3-compatible storage for files and the continuous database backup, see Storage, S3 and backups.
– Optionally a PostgreSQL database instead of SQLite, see PostgreSQL. How much hardware you need for how many people is under Sizing.

en.heading: With Docker Compose
paragraphs: Flowplan is open source (AGPL-3.0). The ready-made image is in the GitHub Container Registry, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64:
Tag Content
ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan:latest The latest version (release)
ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan:0.7.0 A fixed version (currently 0.7.0), also as :0.7 and :0
ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan:beta The latest manually built development state, or a release if that is newer – for trying out, not for production
– Download the Compose file and the example configuration:

``bash mkdir flowplan && cd flowplan curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yannicschuller/flowplan/main/compose.yaml curl -o .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yannicschuller/flowplan/main/.env.example ``
– In .env, set at least the public address:
``dotenv APP_URL=https://flowplan.example.com # Recommended once the address is reachable from the internet: openssl rand -hex 24 FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN= ``

With FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN you create the first account via https://flowplan.example.com/register?setup=; without the link a new instance offers neither sign-up nor restore. If the token is missing and APP_URL is not a local address, Flowplan warns at start in the log and on the setup screen.

For single sign-on also set OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET and OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP (see Sign-in); for e-mails (invitations, forgotten passwords) the SMTP_* values from the configuration.
– Start it:
``bash docker compose up -d ``

The container listens on port 3000 (bound to 127.0.0.1 only in the Compose file, so that the proxy sits in front of it). The volume flowplan-data on /app/data holds all content independently of the container. Choose a fixed version with FLOWPLAN_VERSION=0.7.0 in .env.
> An instance opens with the sign-in page. The website flowplan.org and this documentation are separate projects; the hosted instance runs at app.flowplan.org.

en.heading: Build the image yourself
paragraphs: From the source code (github.com/yannicschuller/flowplan):
git clone https://github.com/yannicschuller/flowplan.git && cd flowplan
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build
Or without Compose:
docker build -t flowplan:latest .
docker run -d --name flowplan \
-v flowplan-data:/app/data \
--env-file .env \
flowplan:latest

Build arguments: PG_CLIENT_MAJOR (default 18) chooses the version of pg_dump, pg_restore and psql in the image – at least your PostgreSQL server's major version (PostgreSQL). FLOWPLAN_SKIP_TYPECHECK=1 is meant for development only: it skips the TypeScript check during the build when it already ran, as in our CI. FLOWPLAN_DEPLOYMENT_ID sets the deployment id (default v-, off: none) that keeps browsers from mixing versions during a rolling update (High availability). {since=0.10.0}

The image contains Node and Litestream for the S3 backup, on Debian 13. There is no real curl; for health checks that call curl inside the container (such as Coolify's HTTP check) a small stand-in is there that does exactly that. {since=0.9.7} Flowplan runs in it as UID 1000 (the user node), or as the user from PUID/PGID when started as root {since=0.10.0} – never as root (Volume permissions).

en.heading: First start
paragraphs: – Open https://flowplan.example.com/api/health – the answer is 200 with "status":"ok".

– Open the address in the browser: a new instance offers Create account. This first account administers the instance. If the address is reachable from the internet, set FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN first and create the account via /register?setup= – otherwise someone could beat you to it (Sign-in). (With single sign-on: Sign in with SSO; administrators are the members of the group in OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP.)
– In the sidebar under Administration, set the instance name, upload limit, sign-ups and the other settings.

Moving or reinstalling? Instead of the first account, the setup screen offers Restore from a backup: upload a backup file or fetch the newest backup from S3 or via SFTP, encrypted ones with the old instance's key. Afterwards you sign in with the accounts of the backup (Restore while setting up). To move from a running instance there is also Moving an instance.

> With SQLite, exactly one instance runs. Several replicas would write to the same SQLite file. Do not simply scale horizontally; when updating, stop the old container before the new one. Several instances only work in cluster mode with PostgreSQL, Redis and S3.

en.heading: Without HTTPS
paragraphs: For trying it out only: Flowplan also runs at a plain http:// address, for example APP_URL=http://192.168.1.20:3000 on your own network. APP_URL must then be exactly that address – with http:// and the port.
The sign-in page and Administration → Instance then show the note "This instance runs without HTTPS". That is fine for a test, not for real use:
– Passwords cross the network unencrypted – anyone on the same network can read them.
– Passkeys, the offline copy, push, and the camera, microphone and clipboard are only available in the browser over HTTPS. Flowplan hides them or says why they are missing.

– The apps for iPhone, iPad and Android connect without HTTPS only to an instance on your local network (e.g. http://192.168.1.20:3000, http://nas or http://nas.local) and warn first. On iPhone and iPad, .lan or .home.arpa names don't work – enter the IP address there. See An instance on your own network without HTTPS.
– Cookies carry no Secure flag, and the browser does not upgrade requests to HTTPS.
At http://localhost or http://127.0.0.1 on your own computer there is no note: browsers treat these addresses like a secure connection.

For real use, put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front (see Coolify and reverse proxies) and change APP_URL to the https:// address. With Caddy two lines are enough; Caddy gets the certificate itself.

> Up to 0.8.0 Flowplan silently required HTTPS: at an http:// address styles and scripts were missing and the registration form simply stayed put. This is fixed – and forms with a password never send credentials in the address bar again.

en.heading: Update
paragraphs: When a newer release exists, the administration shows a notice with the new version number and a link to the changes (turn off with FLOWPLAN_UPDATE_CHECK=false, see Configuration). With the image tag :latest, this is all it takes:
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
With a self-built image, use git pull and docker compose up -d --build instead.
On start, Flowplan migrates the database itself. Make a backup beforehand (see Storage, S3 and backups); going back to an older version after a migration is not supported.

After the update everyone sees New in Flowplan once the next time they open Flowplan: the release notes of every version since the one they last saw – the newest unfolded, older ones folded, grouped into Breaking changes, Security, New, Improved and Bug fixes; breaking changes are highlighted at the top. Close (or Esc) and Settings dismiss the dialog for this version. The notes are part of the image: Flowplan does not ask the internet for them. New accounts start at the running version and see no older notes; accounts from before 0.9.4 see only 0.9.4's notes after updating to it. Beta images (:beta) show the notes up to the version they report – the next release's notes only with that release. Everyone chooses what they get under Settings → Appearance & language → What's new after updates (Light and dark); administrators set the default for new accounts under Administration → Instance (Instance). The complete list of changes is in the changelog on GitHub.

en.heading: Upgrading to 0.7.0
paragraphs: Nothing to do by hand; Flowplan creates the new tables (for idempotency keys and the push relay, among others) on start. What changes for operations:
– API description only when signed in: /api/openapi.json and /api/docs need a sign-in or an API token. Public as before with FLOWPLAN_PUBLIC_API_DOCS=true (see OpenAPI and SDKs).
– A shorter health check: without a token, /api/health only answers {"service":"flowplan","status":"ok"}; the details come with FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN (see Health check).

– Push to the apps through the push relay: notifications to the apps go end-to-end encrypted through push.flowplan.org. APP_URL must be the public HTTPS address and outgoing HTTPS to the relay possible – see Push relay.
– Usage statistics: monitoring counts requests, active people and storage – numbers only. Switch it off with FLOWPLAN_METRICS=off or in the administration (see Statistics).

en.heading: Kubernetes (Helm)
paragraphs: The chart lives in the repository at deploy/helm/flowplan. By default Flowplan runs as exactly one pod (SQLite) with a volume for /app/data; updates replace the pod with a short downtime (strategy Recreate). The chart installs the Flowplan version of its appVersion; choose another with --set image.tag=…. Everything about it – several pods, moving from SQLite, updates, backups, troubleshooting – is on the page Kubernetes. {since=0.10.0}
kubectl create namespace flowplan
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-env \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
helm install flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan \
--set appUrl=https://flowplan.example.org \
--set existingSecret=flowplan-env \
--set ingress.enabled=true \
--set ingress.hosts[0].host=flowplan.example.org

– Set OIDC, SMTP and S3 via oidc., smtp. and s3.*; secrets only in existingSecret (keys are the names of the environment variables) – the chart takes none as a value. {since=0.10.0} Further variables via env.
– appUrl is required (or taken from the first ingress host).

– The chart generates a random FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN in the Secret flowplan-setup (kept across upgrades; your own Secret via setupToken.existingSecret). {since=0.10.0} Create the first account with the setup link helm install prints at the end: https://flowplan.example.org/register?setup=; read the token with kubectl -n flowplan get secret flowplan-setup -o jsonpath='{.data.FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN}' base64 -d.
– Use a block or local volume, not NFS (SQLite).
– Health checks use /api/health; the pod runs as user 1000 without extra privileges on a read-only root file system. {since=0.10.0} helm test flowplan checks that it answers.
– The volume is kept on uninstall.
– To update: git pull in the repository, then helm upgrade flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan -f my-values.yaml.

The chart's README explains every value. Several pods with PostgreSQL, Redis and S3 (cluster.enabled=true): see Cluster mode. The database role in DATABASE_URL should own the database but not be a superuser (Role without superuser rights).

en.heading: Without Docker
paragraphs: Node.js 22.13 or newer (the image uses Node 26):
npm ci
npm run build
FLOWPLAN_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/flowplan npm start
For local development, npm run dev is enough. Development mode also offers Open local workspace, a shared example account; production mode has no such access.

en.heading: Next
paragraphs: – Configuration: all environment variables.
– Coolify and reverse proxies: running behind Traefik, Coolify or Pangolin.
– Moving an instance: to another server, with an example for Hetzner Cloud.
– PostgreSQL and cluster mode: for larger teams.

Under Administration → Instance → Features of this instance you switch features off for the whole instance – the same list as in Show and hide features. Unlike there, the feature is then not only hidden but off. Flowplan asks before switching one off.

en.heading: Switching off and on again
paragraphs: – Hidden for everyone, whatever they chose themselves. In their own settings the switch is off, locked and says Switched off for this instance by the administration; the same goes for Features for new accounts.

– The server refuses it: new pages of that kind, its commands, the matching API routes and MCP tools answer 403 with "… switched off on this instance". MCP clients are not even offered the feature's tools.
– No background work: whatever runs in the background for the feature pauses – every round checks the setting again, in cluster mode on every instance.

– What exists stays unchanged: pages of that kind still show in the sidebar, the search and the trash and open read-only, with the notice Switched off on this instance. Renaming, moving, deleting, restoring, exports and backups work as always.
– Public links to such pages show "not available".
Switch the feature on again and everything is as before: nothing was deleted or rebuilt. Every change is in the activity log (admin.modulesOff, such as "off: workflows").
Feature Switched off
Flashcards No flashcard commands and no studying (shared links included); existing Study views show a notice, cards and progress stay. The daily study reminder pauses.
Whiteboards, notebooks, dashboards No new pages of that kind, existing ones read-only; whiteboard templates, racks and facilitation as well as live editing through links are locked.
Journal No new journals and no journal commands; the journal and its day pages read-only.

Workflows No new workflows and no runs. The queue and the schedules do not run, events are not recorded (nothing piles up for later) and webhooks answer 403. What was already queued carries on once switched on; of a missed schedule at most the latest slot runs then, as after a restart.
draw.io The draw.io editor no longer opens; existing diagrams stay in the pages as pictures.
AI Like the master switch under Administration → AI: no AI feature, on-device included. AI properties, the queue and the semantic index pause and are worked off once switched on.
More view types No new views of these types; existing ones stay as they are.
Forms Every form is closed – public ones too – with a notice that forms are switched off on this instance; the Form view shows a notice, answers stay.
Meetings Nothing is recorded, transcribed or summarised, meeting reminders pause. Kept audio can still be deleted and is still removed once its retention ends.

en.page: Overview and review in the journal
paragraphs: Streak, heatmap and tracker history on the journal page, and the review of a week or a month – as numbers, as a page or summarised by AI.

en.page: Overview and review in the journal
en.heading: Overview on the journal page
paragraphs: – Streak: how many days in a row you have written, plus the longest streak, entries and words.
– Heatmap: the last year as squares, the darker the more you wrote. A click opens the day.
– On this day: entries from a week, a month, half a year and whole years ago.
– Last 30 days: the course of every tracker.
– List or calendar: the list shows an excerpt, place, mood and the first photo of each day; the calendar shows a month with photos as backgrounds.

en.page: Overview and review in the journal
en.heading: Review
paragraphs: Review sums up a week or a month: days, words, completed and still open tasks, tracker averages, places and photos. Copy as Markdown takes the summary along, for example into a weekly report.

en.page: Overview and review in the journal
en.heading: Summarise with AI
paragraphs: Summarise with AI in the review has the AI sum up the week or month shown: highlights and achievements, a chronological overview and what is still open or needs following up – in the interface language. It works from each day's text, the completed and still open tasks, the trackers and places.
– The result appears as a preview first; nothing is saved. Copy, Retry and Discard sit below it.

– Save as page creates a sub-page of the journal, such as "AI summary October 2026", with a note that it was made with AI. There is one such page per journal and period: ask again for the same period and the review offers Open or Create again and replace. Replacing changes the page's content; the previous state stays in the version history.
– A journal with a PIN is closed to the AI, even while it is unlocked. Days closed to the AI (Close pages and spaces to AI) stay out, with everything that belongs to them.
– The button is only there when summaries are available to you and the AI may read the journal; otherwise it is greyed out or missing. The AI reads long periods in parts.

en.page: Overview and review in the journal
en.heading: Monthly summary
paragraphs: In the review of a month, Create monthly summary creates a normal sub-page of the journal – not a day – and opens it, such as "Monthly summary October 2026". It holds:
– days, words, completed and still open tasks in numbers,
– Highlights: tracker averages, places, photos and the completed tasks with a link to their day,
– Still open: tasks from this month that are still open today, with a link to the day they are on now,
– Days: every day as a link with the beginning of its text.

The page is built from your entries alone, without AI, and can be edited freely afterwards. If the month already has a summary, the review offers Open monthly summary; Create a new one anyway deliberately adds another one.
A journal is a page with one sub-page per day. In the morning today's page is ready, with yesterday's open tasks already on it.

en.heading: Create a journal
paragraphs: New page → Journal. The page shows Today at the top and the past days below it with relative labels such as "Yesterday". The day pages are named after the date automatically, such as "Saturday, 26 September 2026".

en.heading: How a day comes about
paragraphs: – When a new day is opened for the first time, Flowplan creates its page. The day starts at midnight in your time zone.

– Open tasks from the last day move over – including nested sub-tasks. This includes tasks in progress [/], deferred ones [>] and those with another Obsidian symbol such as [?]; done and cancelled [-] tasks stay on their day, as do empty tasks without text. A small ↻ at the corner of the checkbox shows that a task was carried over from an earlier day.
– Completed tasks and the rest of the text stay on their day.
– Empty days disappear: if a day got nothing of its own besides carried-over tasks, it is removed again on the next day. This way the journal only contains days on which something happened.

{since=0.10.0} A day listing something under Completed this day (as the person opening the journal sees it: Only mine or All, their time zone) stays. A workflow writing into a day (Append to journal day) never removes the day before.

{since=0.10.0} An empty day goes to the trash, restorable, without the tasks that moved on. Opening its date again, or a workflow writing into it, brings that day back; a day you deleted yourself stays in the trash.

en.heading: Create the day's page: automatically or on the first write
paragraphs: Under Set up journal → Days you decide when today's page is created:
– Automatically (default): as described above, as soon as the day starts and the journal or the app is opened.

– On the first write: Today first shows a draft with the template and the tasks that would be carried over from the last day. Nothing is saved yet – the top bar says "Draft – created when you start writing". Only the first keystroke, a ticked task, a tracker value, a place or a file creates the page. Until then carried-over tasks stay on their day, and the draft appears neither in the sidebar nor in search, graph or export.

The draft is the same on every device: if two devices start writing at the same time, exactly one page is created and both texts end up in it. If what the day starts with changed in the meantime (for example because a task was ticked yesterday on another device), Flowplan opens the stored page and says so. Text typed offline stays on the device and creates the page as soon as the connection is back.

Without a connection, Today opens even when the draft could not be loaded: you write into an entry on this device, and its text goes into the day once it is created (see What works offline). {since=0.10.0}
Every day remembers which version of the template it was created from. A day that only holds that template counts as empty even if the template was changed later.

en.heading: Remove empty days
paragraphs: Set up journal → Days → Find empty days lists old days on which nothing was written: only the template, no open tasks of its own, no tracker values or places, no files, comments, sub-pages, favourites, shares or links from other pages, title and icon unchanged (upper/lower case or spaces do not count as a change). Today always stays. You untick what should stay and move the rest with Move … days to the trash – days can be restored from there. Flowplan never removes or merges old days on its own.

en.heading: Daily template
paragraphs: Set up journal (gear on the journal page) → Template: every new day starts with this content, such as "Grateful for", "Focus today" and "Evening review". Ready-made templates are available (gratitude & focus, 5-minute journal, work log, daily review); Save today as template {since=0.9.8} makes the current day's content the template for every new day. Tasks from the template come back every day and are not carried over in addition. A day that only holds the template counts as empty and disappears like any empty day.

Choose from templates … {since=0.9.8} lists your saved document templates that apply in the journal's space: those of this space, those of the whole workspace and your private ones. Choosing one copies its content into the daily template. Later changes to the saved template don't change the journal – only when you choose it again. Database templates and templates of other spaces are not offered. Remove clears the daily template; new days then start empty.

Carried-over tasks (also under Template) decides where the open tasks of the day before go in a new day: At the top (the default, before the template), After the template or Below the heading … – the template's headings are offered. With a heading, the task list goes directly below it, before whatever the template puts there. If the template no longer has the heading, the tasks go after the template. This applies to days created automatically as well as to the draft with On the first write.

en.heading: Trackers, place and appointments
paragraphs: Above every day there is a bar:
– Trackers: mood (😞 to 😄), scales from 1 to 5, numbers with a unit (e.g. sleep in hours) or yes/no (e.g. sport). You decide which ones exist under Set up journal → Trackers.
– Place: enter freely; Location also stores the device's coordinates with a link to the map.

– Appointments: records of all databases with a date that you may see, including recurrences. Under Set up journal → Calendar you can also add a calendar via an iCal link (Google, Apple, Outlook, Nextcloud …).
In the settings under Day bar, place and appointments can be switched off for the whole journal.

en.heading: Completed this day
paragraphs: Below every day, Completed this day lists the database records that were completed that day and the tasks ticked off in a document that day – including those of your page "Tasks" from My tasks – each with the time, a link and the name of the database or page. Tasks carry a small task symbol. The list is worked out each time the day opens and is not copied into the day; tick a record off elsewhere (in another tab, too) and it is there when you come back.
– A record counts on the day it was last completed, and only while it is still done by its database's done rule – reopen it and it leaves the list. The day follows your time zone.

– All / Only mine at the top of the list: Only mine (the default) shows the records you completed yourself and those a person property assigns to you, whoever ticked them off. When an automation completes a record, it counts for the person who set up the automation. The choice is yours for this journal, on all devices.

– Only records you may see appear – no private records of others, nothing from locked journals or encrypted spaces. On a day with nothing completed, the list is missing; beyond 100 records it ends with "and … more".
– It can be switched off for the whole journal under Set up journal → Day bar → Completed this day (on by default).

– A task counts on the day it was last ticked off, and only while it is done – reopened or Cancelled, it drops out. Tasks of the day itself are in the day already and do not appear here. With Only mine, the tasks you ticked off or that are given to you count.
– If you change the text of a completed task, it stays in the list – with its new text.

en.heading: Meeting notes
paragraphs: Next to every appointment there is Create meeting note. Flowplan creates a page below the journal – with the title and date of the appointment, the Attendees, an Agenda, Notes and Tasks – and opens it. Afterwards the appointment shows Open note.

– Attendees: from the connected Google or Outlook calendar, from the iCal link and from person properties of the record. Whoever is a member of the workspace with that e-mail address is mentioned; others are listed with name and address.
– Tasks with @person show up for that person in My tasks right away.
– For records of a database the note links the record. A PIN lock of the journal also covers its meeting notes.
– The same outline is available as the template Meeting note under Templates → Meetings.

en.heading: In the sidebar
paragraphs: Even after years with thousands of days, the journal stays short in the sidebar. Below the journal you find:
– Today – also when today's page has not been created yet; a click opens the day,
– the last 7 days,
– All days … with the number of all days: opens the journal page at its list or calendar.
Other sub-pages of the journal (such as meeting notes or monthly summaries) follow below as usual.
Under Set up journal → Days you choose for each journal which days appear in the sidebar:
– None
– Last 7 days (the default)

– Grouped by year and month: as above, older days in addition in folders by year and month, such as "October 2026 · 18". The folders only exist in the sidebar, they are not pages – you cannot drag anything into them.
– All: every single day, as before.

When a day is open, the sidebar always shows it – also when it is older than 7 days; in the grouped view its year and month unfold. Days can still be dragged, and the arrow keys work in the folders too (→ opens, ← closes or jumps to the folder above).

en.heading: From day to day
paragraphs: Above every day page there is a bar:
– ← Previous day and Next day → jump to the previous or next day with an entry – gaps are skipped.
– Today opens today's day.
– The month (such as "October 2026") opens a small calendar: days with an entry are highlighted and can be opened. The arrow keys move by a day or a week, Page ↑/Page ↓ by a month; Esc closes it.

– Fill in an earlier day: if you may write in the journal, a past day without an entry can be chosen in the calendar too (Create entry). Flowplan creates the page for that day and opens it – with the daily template, but without carrying over open tasks. Today works as usual; days after today stay locked, as do days whose page is in the trash and a journal behind its PIN. {since=0.9.7}

From anywhere, ⌘ ⌥ Y (Windows/Linux: Ctrl Alt Y) or the command Journal: Today in the quick search (⌘ K) takes you to today – of the journal used last. With several journals the quick search offers one entry per journal. The shortcut can be changed (see Keyboard shortcuts).
The streak, heatmap and tracker history on the journal page and the review of a week or a month are described in Overview and review in the journal.

en.heading: PIN lock
paragraphs: Under Set up journal → Lock, a PIN of 6 to 8 digits protects the journal (shorter PINs set earlier keep working): days, search, previews and images stay hidden until the PIN is entered. After 15 minutes or with the lock button it locks itself again. After five wrong attempts there is a five-minute pause, after twenty in one day it is over until the next day – across server restarts too. When another person enters a wrong PIN five times, the person who created the journal gets a notification. Only the person who created the journal and the workspace owners may set or change a PIN. Changing or removing it requires the current PIN – a wrong one counts against the same limits as when unlocking, and after five wrong ones the person who created the journal is notified as well. If the PIN is forgotten, owners can remove it on the lock screen with Reset PIN. Like other important steps, they confirm this once more – with their password, a code from the authenticator app or a passkey, or, without any of these, with a sign-in no more than ten minutes ago. The reset is recorded in the activity log and the journal's creator is notified. The lock also covers sub-pages of days, databases below the journal (their records, relations, calendar subscriptions and CalDAV) as well as export, the content archive, comments and duplicating – unlock first for those. It protects against glances but is no encryption: whoever has access to the server's backups sees the content.

A journal with a PIN stays private: setting the PIN revokes every share link and publication of the journal and the pages below it, switches off public forms of its databases and takes the journal out of links and publications of pages above it. The message after locking says how many there were; the security log records it. No new links, publications or public forms can be created for a journal with a PIN – not even while it is unlocked. Sharing or publishing a page above it with its sub-pages leaves the journal out. Forms for members only stay.

en.heading: If today's page was deleted
paragraphs: If today's page is in the trash, the journal says so and offers Create again (a fresh page for today; with On the first write a new draft) or Restore from trash.

en.heading: Days in lists, search, graph and export
paragraphs: A journal soon has hundreds of days. So that they do not crowd out other pages:
– Search and @ mentions: days come after all other hits. The filter Without journal days in the quick search leaves them out completely (it stays on for the next search).

– @heute, @gestern and @2026-10-27 (also @today, @yesterday) insert a link to that day of the journal while writing – the journal in the page's space, otherwise the one written in last. Today works as when opening the journal: the page is created or, with On the first write, the link goes to the draft. Days without an entry cannot be linked.
– Graph: under Journal days the graph hides the days, shows one dot per month (default) or each day.
– Counting: the home page, space settings and administration count days separately, such as "120 pages · 340 journal days".
– Export: in the Markdown ZIP, the scheduled export and Git, days sort by path in their journal's folder under 2026/10/2026-10-27.md – see Import, export and versions.
Journals behind a PIN you have not entered appear in none of these – not even in the numbers.

en.heading: Tips
paragraphs: – /todo or [] + space creates tasks that move along. They also appear under My tasks, without any @mention.
– Day pages are normal documents: headings, tables, images, mentions – everything works.
– Journals can be shared like any page. Whoever may only read sees the days but does not create any.
– The quick search finds entries across all days; Without journal days hides them.

en.heading: Workflows
paragraphs: The workflow trigger New journal day starts a workflow when a day's page is created – so when the day is first opened or written in (or automatically, if the journal creates days itself), not at midnight. For fixed times there is the Schedule trigger. Journals with a PIN are closed to workflows.

With the step Append to journal day, a workflow writes into a day: today, yesterday or a given date, at the end of the day or below a heading. If the day does not exist yet, the workflow creates it the way opening it would – with the template and the carried-over tasks. More under Workflow nodes.
All shortcuts at a glance. On Windows and Linux, Ctrl stands for ⌘ and Alt for ⌥.
Letter shortcuts also work with non-Latin keyboard layouts (Cyrillic, Greek …): the key that carries the Latin letter counts – with a Russian layout, ⌘ Z is the key with “Я”. {since=0.9.8}

en.heading: Everywhere
paragraphs: Shortcut Effect
⌘ K Quick search

⌘ F Find on the page: marks every match, Enter or ⇧ Enter jumps to the next or previous one, Esc closes. Selected text becomes the query. Also works in the desktop app and the apps; on a whiteboard it searches the board.
⌘ N New page
⌘ ⌥ N Quick capture (record in the capture database)

en.heading: In this documentation
paragraphs: / jumps into the search, arrow keys choose a hit, Enter opens it.
Flowplan on Kubernetes with the Helm chart: from one pod with SQLite on a volume to several pods with high availability against PostgreSQL, Redis and S3.

en.heading: Two ways to run it
paragraphs: One pod Several pods (cluster mode)
For up to about 20 people active at the same time more people, updates without downtime, losing a node
Data SQLite and files on a volume (PVC) PostgreSQL, files in S3, Redis between the pods
Updates short downtime (Recreate) rolling, pod by pod
Example values values-small.yaml values-ha.yaml
How many pods and how much CPU and memory: see Sizing. What the pods share and how they work together: see Cluster mode.

en.heading: Requirements
paragraphs: – Kubernetes 1.23 or newer, Helm 3, an ingress controller (ingress-nginx is set up by default) and a certificate for your address (e.g. cert-manager).
– One pod: a block or local volume (ReadWriteOnce) – no NFS, SQLite can break on it.

– Several pods: PostgreSQL 16 or newer, Redis (tested with 7, no persistence needed) and an S3 bucket (MinIO, Garage, AWS …). The chart does not install any of them – use managed services or their own charts or operators. The PostgreSQL role should own the database but not be a superuser (Role without superuser rights); PostgreSQL's max_connections must stay above replicas × (cluster.poolSize + 3).
> The chart takes no secret as a value. Passwords, keys and connection strings go into Secrets you create; the chart only names them. Only the setup token can be generated by the chart.

en.heading: Install with Helm
paragraphs: The chart lives in the repository under deploy/helm/flowplan; its README describes every value. One pod:
git clone https://github.com/yannicschuller/flowplan.git && cd flowplan
kubectl create namespace flowplan
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-env \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
cp deploy/helm/flowplan/values-small.yaml my-values.yaml   # address, host, SMTP, S3
helm install flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan -f my-values.yaml
The chart creates the Secret flowplan-setup with a random setup token, keeps it on upgrades and does not delete it on uninstall. Several pods:
kubectl create namespace flowplan
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-cluster \
--from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgres://flowplan:<password>@postgres:5432/flowplan' \
--from-literal=REDIS_URL='redis://:<password>@redis-master:6379/0'
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-s3 \
--from-literal=S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<key-id>' \
--from-literal=S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<secret>'
# The keys every pod shares (push keys: npx web-push generate-vapid-keys)
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-keys \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
--from-literal=WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY='<public VAPID key>' \
--from-literal=WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY='<private VAPID key>'
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-env \
--from-literal=OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET='<client secret>' \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 24)"
kubectl -n flowplan create secret generic flowplan-setup \
--from-literal=FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 20)"
cp deploy/helm/flowplan/values-ha.yaml my-values.yaml   # address, hosts, bucket, replicas
helm install flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan -f my-values.yaml
Before the pods start, a Job brings the database schema up to this version. A pod is ready once its schema and data steps are done.
Then:
helm test flowplan -n flowplan
echo "https://flowplan.example.org/register?setup=$(kubectl -n flowplan get secret flowplan-setup \
-o jsonpath='{.data.FLOWPLAN_SETUP_TOKEN}' | base64 -d)"
Open the link and create the first account – it administers the instance. Keep a copy of FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY apart from the backups: without it, encrypted files and backups cannot be read.

en.heading: What the chart sets up
paragraphs: – Probes: one pod on /api/health; several pods with startup and liveness on /api/health/live and readiness on /api/health/ready – ready only once the schema and the data steps are done and the database and the bucket answer. Redis does not count by default (cluster.readyRequire: database,objectStorage): if Redis fails, every pod stays in the rotation and editing goes on.
– Ingress: for ingress-nginx, no buffering, read and send timeouts of an hour for the live connections, and uploads up to ingress.bodySize (110 MB). Other controllers: see the chart's README.
– Security: the pod runs as user 1000 without privileges on a read-only root file system; /tmp, /app/.next/cache and /home/node are emptyDirs.
– Resources: per pod 1 CPU and 2 GiB requested, 4 GiB at most (from Sizing); no CPU limit, as throttling slows live editing.
– Several pods: rolling updates without an unavailable pod, a PodDisruptionBudget, pods spread over nodes, a cache per pod (cluster.cacheSizeLimit) that keeps itself below 70 % of its limit.
– Optional: a ServiceMonitor for the Prometheus Operator (metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled) and a NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.enabled).

Not part of the chart: PostgreSQL, Redis or MinIO as subcharts, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler and separate worker pods – every pod serves requests and takes jobs from the queues, the leader the timed ones.

en.heading: Moving from one SQLite container
paragraphs: You bring the data into PostgreSQL with the migration tool and the files into the bucket with the S3 mirror of the single container – both without losing anything; only the copy itself needs a short downtime.
– Same version. Bring the single pod to the Flowplan version the cluster will run (helm upgrade with the new chart or image.tag) and let it start once.

– Files into the bucket. Turn on S3 in the single pod (s3.bucket, s3.endpoint, the keys in s3.existingSecret or existingSecret) and wait until every file is there: Administration → Storage & backup, or objectStorage.pending at 0 in /api/health. Use the same bucket and prefix in the cluster later.

– Keep the keys. Without FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY and push keys, the single container made them itself. Take them from its data folder into the Secret flowplan-keys: the content of secrets.key as FLOWPLAN_SECRETS_KEY (in addition to a FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY), publicKey/privateKey of web-push-keys.json as WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY/WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY:
``bash kubectl -n flowplan exec deploy/flowplan -- cat /app/data/secrets.key kubectl -n flowplan exec deploy/flowplan -- cat /app/data/web-push-keys.json ``
– Prepare the target: an empty PostgreSQL database and a role that owns it (Requirements), and the Secret flowplan-cluster as above.
– Back up: Administration → Storage & backup → Whole instance → Download.
– Stop Flowplan: kubectl -n flowplan scale deploy/flowplan --replicas=0. The volume stays.
– Copy and verify with a pod on the same volume (flowplan-data is the chart's PVC):
```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: flowplan-migrate spec: restartPolicy: Never securityContext: { runAsUser: 1000, runAsGroup: 1000, fsGroup: 1000 } containers:
– name: migrate image: ghcr.io/yannicschuller/flowplan:0.10.0 command: ["node", "/app/scripts/db-migrate.mjs"] args: ["--from", "sqlite:/app/data/flowplan.sqlite", "--to", "$(DATABASE_URL)"] env:
– name: DATABASE_URL valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: flowplan-cluster, key: DATABASE_URL } } volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /app/data }] volumes:
– name: data persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: flowplan-data } ```

kubectl -n flowplan apply -f migrate.yaml, then kubectl -n flowplan logs -f flowplan-migrate. The last line must read verified: every table has the same rows. Delete the pod afterwards. Details and options of the tool: Switching the database.

– Switch to cluster mode: helm upgrade flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan -f my-values.yaml with cluster.enabled: true and the same bucket. The PVC is kept – delete it only once the cluster runs and its first backup exists.
– Check: sign in, open a page with images, search, and under Administration → Monitoring → System see the pods, the leader and PostgreSQL.

en.heading: Updates
paragraphs: git pull
helm upgrade flowplan deploy/helm/flowplan -n flowplan -f my-values.yaml

With several pods, the schema Job runs first (it only adds, never removes), then the pods are replaced one by one: a new pod only gets requests once it is ready, an old one stops only after that. Browsers of a stopping pod reconnect to another one by themselves. If the Job fails, nothing is replaced – kubectl -n flowplan logs job/flowplan-schema says why. Going back with helm rollback works: an older version runs on the newer schema.

A pod that stops gets terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30): open requests and running jobs finish, uploads still under way reach the bucket, the lead goes to another pod. For long imports or exports, raise the value.

en.heading: Backups
paragraphs: – One pod: as with Docker – scheduled backups in the administration, with S3 also Litestream (Storage, S3 and backups). Back up the volume as well, if your platform can.

– Several pods: PostgreSQL holds all data: the scheduled backups in the administration are pg_dump archives in the bucket (Backups with pg_dump); add your provider's backups or point-in-time recovery. The files are in the bucket – turn on versioning there or replicate it. Redis needs no backup.
– Always: keep the Secrets (above all FLOWPLAN_ENCRYPTION_KEY and the push keys) apart from the backups.
– Restoring a backup replaces every table: scale to one pod first (cluster.replicas: 1), restore, then scale up again.

en.heading: Scaling
paragraphs: Set cluster.replicas and run helm upgrade – one pod per about 25 people active at the same time, plus a spare. More pods need more database connections: each pod opens up to cluster.poolSize plus three of its own. The PodDisruptionBudget (cluster.podDisruptionBudget.minAvailable) keeps pods running while nodes are drained; keep it below replicas.

What to watch: response times and CPU per pod under Administration → Monitoring, "waiting" connections under System (raise cluster.poolSize or add pods), and with Prometheus the metrics of each pod (instance_id label; the installation's figures only from the leader).

en.heading: Limits
paragraphs: – Restores and instance moves with one pod – see Backups.
– Imports are staged in the pod's cache (cluster.cacheSizeLimit, 5 GiB) and in the bucket; for imports of several gigabytes raise the limit and ingress.bodySize.

– Redis: one address only, no Sentinel or Redis Cluster. While Redis is away, changes between pods arrive with the browser's next check (within about 20 seconds) instead of at once, and rate limits count per pod.
– Meeting notes: a recording is transcribed by the pod that received its end; if that pod stops meanwhile, start the processing again in the block.
– Not tested on every platform: the chart is checked against the Kubernetes API; report what your controller needs.

en.heading: Troubleshooting
paragraphs: Symptom Cause and fix

Pods stay "not ready" Ask the pod what is missing: kubectl -n flowplan exec deploy/flowplan -- node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health/ready',{headers:{authorization:'Bearer '+process.env.FLOWPLAN_METRICS_TOKEN}}).then(r=>r.text()).then(console.log)" – opening names a failed data step or an older schema, database and objectStorage their errors.
The schema Job fails kubectl -n flowplan logs job/flowplan-schema: usually the address, the password or missing rights of the role.
Pods do not start: "Cluster mode cannot start" A Secret or key is missing; the log lists every problem at once.
Live changes come late or the connection drops every few seconds The ingress buffers or cuts the stream: with ingress-nginx keep ingress.nginxDefaults; for others see the chart's README.
Uploads fail with 503 The bucket does not answer – a file is only stored once it is in the bucket. Check the endpoint, keys and network policy.
Pods are evicted ("ephemeral-storage") The cache or /tmp is too small for large files: raise cluster.cacheSizeLimit or scratch.tmpSizeLimit.
"remaining connection slots are reserved" Too many connections: lower cluster.poolSize or raise max_connections.
"Shutdown: not finished in time" in the log Raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Two-factor sign-in or push works only sometimes The pods have different keys: cluster.keys.existingSecret must be the same Secret for all.

Flowplan is available in 4 languages: German, English, French and Simplified Chinese (简体中文). English also comes as English (US): the same texts, but dates with the month first and weeks starting on Sunday. Further languages can be added without changing the app's code – with any translation tool that understands JSON files.
> Help bring Flowplan to your language: at translate.flowplan.org you translate right in the browser, signed in with GitHub – here’s how.

en.heading: Choosing a language
paragraphs: Flowplan follows your browser's language; languages Flowplan does not know show English. Under Settings → Appearance & language → Language you pick a language (with its flag) from the list – it then applies on all devices, also to e-mails and push notifications; Automatic (follows the browser) undoes the choice and picks English (US) for browsers set to US English (en-US), English for other English browsers. On the sign-in page the small button in the footer (e.g. 🇬🇧 EN) opens a menu with all languages.

Dates, times and numbers follow the language (French: fr-FR, e.g. “15 oct. 2026” and “2 400,5”; Chinese: zh-CN, e.g. “2026年10月15日”). Calculations in notes use the decimal comma in French as well. Calendars start the week on Sunday in English (US) and on Monday in every other language – unless the view sets its own week start.

What you create yourself – pages, databases, properties – stays in the language it was made in. Templates and example content exist in German and English; French and Chinese accounts get the English ones.

en.heading: Help translate
paragraphs: At translate.flowplan.org the community translates Flowplan right in the browser – no Git, no tools of your own, no need to touch the catalogues. It covers the texts of the web app, the app for iPhone, iPad and Android (with widgets, Siri commands and the app store texts) and the desktop app. Today that means French and Simplified Chinese; German and English are the originals and are only shown there. The tool is free, without tracking and open source (flowplan-translate on GitHub).
– Sign in at translate.flowplan.org with GitHub. Browsing and reading need no account.
– Pick a part (e.g. the web app or the App Store texts) and a language.

– Translate texts or improve existing translations. Next to the English original you see the German text and the terms from the glossary; the tool checks placeholders such as {0} and length limits as you type.
– A reviewer (the maintainer) reviews your suggestions. Accepted translations go to Flowplan's repositories as a pull request and reach the apps with the next version.
Translators are credited as co-authors in the pull request and the commit – so your contributions show up on your GitHub profile, too.
Missing a language? Ask for it in a GitHub issue – further languages are added on request.

en.heading: How translation works
paragraphs: German and English sit side by side in the code. Every further language is a catalogue in the app's locales/ folder that maps the English text to its translation:
"Sign in": "Se connecter",
"{0} commented on “{1}”": "{0} a commenté « {1} »"
– locales/en.json lists every text of the app (more than 3,500) and is the source for translation tools. It is generated, not edited by hand.
– {0}, {1} … stand for values such as names or numbers. They have to appear in the translation; their order may change.
– An empty or missing entry shows the English text – so a language can grow step by step, and new texts in the app never break anything.

en.heading: Adding a language
paragraphs: > These steps are for developers who add a language in the app's code. To improve an existing language, translate.flowplan.org is the easier way – and you ask for a new language with an issue.
– Create the catalogue, e.g. for Italian:
``sh npm run i18n -- --add it ``
This creates locales/it.json with every text and empty translations.

– Translate – by hand or with a tool such as Weblate, Crowdin, POEditor or Lokalise (format “JSON key-value” or “i18next JSON”, source file locales/en.json). Machine translation (e.g. DeepL) works as a draft; please keep placeholders and HTML tags unchanged.
– Register the language: in lib/i18n.ts under LANGUAGES with its name and date format (it: { name: "Italiano", tag: "it-IT" }), and import the catalogue in lib/i18n-catalogs.ts.
– Check:
``sh npm run i18n -- --check # progress and wrong placeholders npm run i18n -- --check --missing # what is still missing, with the place in the code ``
The language then appears in the choice on the sign-in page and in the profile, and browsers in that language get it automatically.

en.heading: Keeping catalogues up to date
paragraphs: After texts change in the code, npm run i18n collects all texts again: new ones are added empty to every catalogue, unused ones drop out, existing translations stay. The tests only report missing translations; wrong placeholders make them fail.

In the code, texts are t("Deutsch", "English") in components, tr() outside of them and ct() for content the server creates. Tables of text pairs get a marker so npm run i18n finds them, e.g. // i18n-table: 1 for [German, English] pairs.

en.heading: Text recognition
paragraphs: Text recognition for scanned PDFs and images is separate: it reads German and English, French with FLOWPLAN_OCR_LANGS=fra,eng and Chinese (Simplified) with FLOWPLAN_OCR_LANGS=chi_sim,eng (see Configuration).

For knowledge with hundreds of pages – handbooks, policies, documentation – show spaces as a library: each such space is a shelf, the pages at the top of the space are its books, their sub-pages the chapters. The library in the navigation shows all shelves at a glance and searches them all at once.
More on this topic: Pages and spaces · Sharing and publishing · Members, roles and permissions

en.heading: A space as a library
paragraphs: For documentation with hundreds of pages, show a space as a library: … next to the space → Edit space … → Show as library. There is no second structure: the pages at the top of the space are the books, their sub-pages the chapters, and theirs the pages.
– Sidebar: the space stays collapsed with just Open library below it. A click on the space's name still expands the page tree, to reorder pages.

– Overview: every book is a tile with icon, cover, number of pages and last edit, in the order of the page tree. A click shows the table of contents with collapsible chapters, Start reading and Continue reading (the page of the book you opened last).
– Reading: above every page you see its book and chapter and arrows to the previous and next page in reading order; at the bottom Next leads on.
– Search: the library's search field searches only this space.
– Create: New book on the overview, New chapter in a book, + on a chapter for a page.

You see only pages you may see; journal days are not part of the library. Through the API, space.update with library switches the view, and GET /api/spaces/{spaceId}/library returns the books and chapters.

en.heading: Books and chapters as overviews
paragraphs: Books and chapters work like the compartments of a shelf: they open as an overview, and the editor appears only with a page.
– New book asks for the name only, in a small window – the shelf and the kind are given. Afterwards you see the new book's overview.

– A book's overview shows its title, cover, the number of pages and chapters, Start reading or Continue reading and the table of contents with collapsible chapters. New chapter creates a chapter, New page a page in a chapter you choose; + on a chapter creates the page right there.
